In particular I continued to study the writings of Alexandre Koyré and first encountered those of Emile Meyerson, Hélène Metzger, and Anneliese Maier.1 More clearly than most other recent scholars, this group has shown what it was like to think scientifically in a period when the canons of scientific thought were very different from those current today. Though I increasingly question a few of their particular historical interpretations, their works, together with A. O. Lovejoy’s Great Chain of Being, have been second only to primary source materials in shaping my conception of what the history of scientific ideas can be.

然而，那些年我的大部分时间都花在了探索一些看似与科学史无关的领域，但如今的研究却揭示出一些与历史学当时引起我注意的问题类似的问题。一次偶然的机会，我读到一篇脚注，它引导我了解了让·皮亚杰的实验，这些实验阐明了儿童成长过程中各个阶段的差异以及从一种阶段过渡到另一种阶段的过程。2

Much of my time in those years, however, was spent exploring fields without apparent relation to history of science but in which research now discloses problems like the ones history was bringing to my attention. A footnote encountered by chance led me to the experiments by which Jean Piaget has illuminated both the various worlds of the growing child and the process of transition from one to the next.2

一位同事让我阅读一些关于知觉心理学的论文，特别是格式塔心理学家的研究；另一位同事则向我介绍了……这让我接触到了B.L. Whorf关于语言对世界观影响的思考；而W.V.O. Quine则为我开启了分析哲学与综合哲学之区分的哲学谜题。3这正是研究员协会所允许的那种随机探索，也正是通过它，我才得以发现路德维克·弗莱克那部几乎无人知晓的专著《科学论题的起源与发展》（巴塞尔，1935），这篇论文预示了我许多自己的想法。弗莱克的著作，连同另一位青年研究员弗朗西斯·X. Sutton的评论，让我意识到这些想法或许需要置于科学共同体的社会学框架下进行探讨。尽管读者在下文中很少会发现对这些著作或对话的引用，但我对它们的感激之情远非我现在能够重现或评价的。

One of my colleagues set me to reading papers in the psychology of perception, particularly the Gestalt psychologists; another introduced me to B. L. Whorf’s speculations about the effect of language on world view; and W. V. O. Quine opened for me the philosophical puzzles of the analytic-synthetic distinction.3 That is the sort of random exploration that the Society of Fellows permits, and only through it could I have encountered Ludwik Fleck’s almost unknown monograph, Entstehung und Entwicklung einer wissenschaftlichen Tatsache (Basel, 1935), an essay that anticipates many of my own ideas. Together with a remark from another Junior Fellow, Francis X. Sutton, Fleck’s work made me realize that those ideas might require to be set in the sociology of the scientific community. Though readers will find few references to either these works or conversations below, I am indebted to them in more ways than I can now reconstruct or evaluate.

在我担任初级研究员的最后一年，受邀前往波士顿的洛厄尔研究所讲学，这为我提供了一个初次实践我仍在发展中的科学理念的机会。1951年3月，我发表了一系列共八场的公开讲座，主题为“物理理论的探索”。次年，我开始教授科学史，在接下来的近十年里，由于我从未系统地研究过这个领域，教学本身就充满了挑战，几乎没有时间去清晰地阐述最初引导我进入这个领域的那些想法。然而幸运的是，这些想法为我后来的高级教学提供了隐性的指导方向和问题框架。因此，我应该感谢我的学生们，他们教会了我许多宝贵的经验，不仅让我认识到我的观点是可行的，也让我学会了如何有效地表达这些观点。同样的问题和指导方向，也为我自研究员任期结束以来发表的大部分以历史为主、看似风格迥异的研究论文赋予了统一性。其中一些论文探讨了形而上学在创造性科学研究中所扮演的重要角色。另一些人则考察了那些坚持与新理论相悖的旧理论的人是如何积累和吸收新理论的实验基础的。在此过程中，他们描述了这种类型的……我在下文中将这种发展称为新理论或发现的“出现”。除此之外，还有其他类似的联系。

During my last year as a Junior Fellow, an invitation to lecture for the Lowell Institute in Boston provided a first chance to try out my still developing notion of science. The result was a series of eight public lectures, delivered during March, 1951, on “The Quest for Physical Theory.” In the next year I began to teach history of science proper, and for almost a decade the problems of instructing in a field I had never systematically studied left little time for explicit articulation of the ideas that had first brought me to it. Fortunately, however, those ideas proved a source of implicit orientation and of some problem-structure for much of my more advanced teaching. I therefore have my students to thank for invaluable lessons both about the viability of my views and about the techniques appropriate to their effective communication. The same problems and orientation give unity to most of the dominantly historical, and apparently diverse, studies I have published since the end of my fellowship. Several of them deal with the integral part played by one or another metaphysic in creative scientific research. Others examine the way in which the experimental bases of a new theory are accumulated and assimilated by men committed to an incompatible older theory. In the process they describe the type of development that I have below called the “emergence” of a new theory or discovery. There are other such ties besides.

本文的最后阶段始于1958-59年受邀前往行为科学高级研究中心进行为期一年的研究。我得以再次全身心投入到下文讨论的问题中。更重要的是，在以社会科学家为主的群体中度过这一年，让我面对着一些意想不到的问题，这些问题涉及社会科学家群体与我之前接受训练的自然科学家群体之间的差异。尤其令我震惊的是，社会科学家之间在合法科学问题的本质和方法论方面存在着数量之多、程度之深的公开分歧。无论是历史经验还是个人经历，都让我怀疑自然科学的实践者是否比社会科学领域的同行拥有更确凿或更持久的答案。然而，不知何故，天文学、物理学、化学或生物学的实践通常不会像如今心理学家或社会学家那样，引发关于基本原理的争论。为了探寻这种差异的根源，我意识到了科学研究中“范式”的作用，我后来将“范式”称为“范式”。我认为“范式”是指那些被普遍认可的科学成就，它们在一段时间内为实践者群体提供了模型问题和解决方案。一旦我理解了这一点，本文的初稿便迅速成型。

The final stage in the development of this essay began with an invitation to spend the year 1958–59 at the Center for Advanced Studies in the Behavioral Sciences. Once again I was able to give undivided attention to the problems discussed below. Even more important, spending the year in a community composed predominantly of social scientists confronted me with unanticipated problems about the differences between such communities and those of the natural scientists among whom I had been trained. Particularly, I was struck by the number and extent of the overt disagreements between social scientists about the nature of legitimate scientific problems and methods. Both history and acquaintance made me doubt that practitioners of the natural sciences possess firmer or more permanent answers to such questions than their colleagues in social science. Yet, somehow, the practice of astronomy, physics, chemistry, or biology normally fails to evoke the controversies over fundamentals that today often seem endemic among, say, psychologists or sociologists. Attempting to discover the source of that difference led me to recognize the role in scientific research of what I have since called “paradigms.” These I take to be universally recognized scientific achievements that for a time provide model problems and solutions to a community of practitioners. Once that piece of my puzzle fell into place, a draft of this essay emerged rapidly.

该草稿后续的演变历程无需在此赘述，但必须简要提及它最终经多次修订后保留下来的形式。在初稿完成并经过大幅修改之前，我曾预期该手稿将仅作为《统一科学百科全书》的一个卷册出版。这部开创性著作的编辑们先是征集了我的稿件，然后严格要求我履行承诺，最后以非凡的技巧和耐心等待最终成果。我非常感谢他们，尤其是查尔斯·莫里斯，感谢他给予我必要的推动，并就最终的手稿提出了宝贵的建议。然而，由于《百科全书》的篇幅限制，我不得不以极其精炼和概括的方式呈现我的观点。形式上。尽管后来的事件在一定程度上放宽了这些限制，使得同时独立出版成为可能，但这部作品仍然是一篇论文，而不是我的主题最终需要的完整著作。

The subsequent history of that draft need not be recounted here, but a few words must be said about the form that it has preserved through revisions. Until a first version had been completed and largely revised, I anticipated that the manuscript would appear exclusively as a volume in the Encyclopedia of Unified Science. The editors of that pioneering work had first solicited it, then held me firmly to a commitment, and finally waited with extraordinary tact and patience for a result. I am much indebted to them, particularly to Charles Morris, for wielding the essential goad and for advising me about the manuscript that resulted. Space limits of the Encyclopedia made it necessary, however, to present my views in an extremely condensed and schematic form. Though subsequent events have somewhat relaxed those restrictions and have made possible simultaneous independent publication, this work remains an essay rather than the full-scale book my subject will ultimately demand.

由于我最根本的目标是促使人们改变对熟悉数据的认知和评价方式，因此，本文初稿的概括性呈现方式并非缺点。相反，那些自身研究已为本文所倡导的这种重新定位做好准备的读者，可能会发现这种散文形式更具启发性，也更容易理解。但它也有不足之处，而这些不足之处或许正是我在开篇就加以阐述的理由，以展现我希望最终在更长版本中纳入的、在范围和深度上的拓展。可供利用的历史证据远比我下文篇幅所能涵盖的要多得多。此外，这些证据来自生物学史和物理学史。我决定在此仅探讨后者，部分原因是出于增强本文连贯性的考虑，部分原因是出于我目前在该领域的专业知识。此外，本文将要阐述的科学观也预示着一些新的研究类型——包括历史学和社会学研究——的潜在价值。例如，异常现象或违反预期的现象如何日益引起科学界的关注，以及反复无法使异常现象符合预期而可能引发的危机，都需要进行详细研究。又如，如果我的观点——即每一次科学革命都会改变经历它的社群的历史视角——是正确的，那么这种视角的转变应该会影响革命后教科书和研究出版物的结构。其中一种影响——研究报告脚注中引用的技术文献分布的变化——应该被研究，作为衡量科学革命发生的一个可能指标。

Since my most fundamental objective is to urge a change in the perception and evaluation of familiar data, the schematic character of this first presentation need be no drawback. On the contrary, readers whose own research has prepared them for the sort of reorientation here advocated may find the essay form both more suggestive and easier to assimilate. But it has disadvantages as well, and these may justify my illustrating at the very start the sorts of extension in both scope and depth that I hope ultimately to include in a longer version. Far more historical evidence is available than I have had space to exploit below. Furthermore, that evidence comes from the history of biological as well as of physical science. My decision to deal here exclusively with the latter was made partly to increase this essay’s coherence and partly on grounds of present competence. In addition, the view of science to be developed here suggests the potential fruitfulness of a number of new sorts of research, both historical and sociological. For example, the manner in which anomalies, or violations of expectation, attract the increasing attention of a scientific community needs detailed study, as does the emergence of the crises that may be induced by repeated failure to make an anomaly conform. Or again, if I am right that each scientific revolution alters the historical perspective of the community that experiences it, then that change of perspective should affect the structure of postrevolutionary textbooks and research publications. One such effect—a shift in the distribution of the technical literature cited in the footnotes to research reports—ought to be studied as a possible index to the occurrence of revolutions.

由于需要大幅精简内容，我不得不放弃对一些重要问题的讨论。例如，我对科学发展中范式转变前后的区分就过于笼统。早期阶段的各个学派之间的竞争，都受到某种重要因素的制约。就像范式一样；虽然我认为这种情况很少见，但在某些情况下，两种范式可以在后期和平共存。仅仅拥有某种范式并不足以构成第二部分所讨论的发展转型的充分条件。更重要的是，除了偶尔的简短提及之外，我没有谈到技术进步或外部社会、经济和知识条件在科学发展中的作用。然而，我们只需看看哥白尼和历法，就能发现外部条件可能有助于将一个单纯的异常现象转化为一场严重的危机。同样的例子也说明了科学之外的条件如何影响那些试图通过提出某种革命性改革来结束危机的人可选择的方案范围。4我认为，明确考虑这些影响并不会改变本文提出的主要论点，但肯定会为理解科学进步增添一个至关重要的分析维度。

The need for drastic condensation has also forced me to forego discussion of a number of major problems. My distinction between the pre- and the post-paradigm periods in the development of a science is, for example, much too schematic. Each of the schools whose competition characterizes the earlier period is guided by something much like a paradigm; there are circumstances, though I think them rare, under which two paradigms can coexist peacefully in the later period. Mere possession of a paradigm is not quite a sufficient criterion for the developmental transition discussed in Section II. More important, except in occasional brief asides, I have said nothing about the role of technological advance or of external social, economic, and intellectual conditions in the development of the sciences. One need, however, look no further than Copernicus and the calendar to discover that external conditions may help to transform a mere anomaly into a source of acute crisis. The same example would illustrate the way in which conditions outside the sciences may influence the range of alternatives available to the man who seeks to end a crisis by proposing one or another revolutionary reform.4 Explicit consideration of effects like these would not, I think, modify the main theses developed in this essay, but it would surely add an analytic dimension of first-rate importance for the understanding of scientific advance.

最后，或许也是最重要的一点，篇幅的限制极大地影响了我对本文以历史视角看待科学的哲学内涵的处理。显然，这些内涵是存在的，我也试图指出并论证其中的主要内涵。但在此过程中，我通常避免详细讨论当代哲学家在相关问题上采取的各种立场。我所表达的怀疑态度，更多是针对某种哲学态度本身，而非针对其任何一种完整阐述的表达方式。因此，一些了解并实践这些已阐述立场的人可能会觉得……我没理解他们的意思。我认为他们错了，但这篇文章的目的并非为了说服他们。如果要做到这一点，就需要写一本篇幅更长、风格截然不同的书。

Finally, and perhaps most important of all, limitations of space have drastically affected my treatment of the philosophical implications of this essay’s historically oriented view of science. Clearly, there are such implications, and I have tried both to point out and to document the main ones. But in doing so I have usually refrained from detailed discussion of the various positions taken by contemporary philosophers on the corresponding issues. Where I have indicated skepticism, it has more often been directed to a philosophical attitude than to any one of its fully articulated expressions. As a result, some of those who know and work within one of those articulated positions may feel that I have missed their point. I think they will be wrong, but this essay is not calculated to convince them. To attempt that would have required a far longer and very different sort of book.

本序开篇的自传片段旨在表明我对学术著作和塑造我思想的机构所怀有的主要感激之情。其余的感激之情，我将在下文中通过引证来表达。然而，无论上文还是下文，都无法完全展现我对众多人士的感激之情，他们的建议和批评曾在不同时期支持和指导了我的学术发展。本文的构思酝酿已久，若要列出所有可能在文中有所体现的人，其篇幅几乎与我的朋友和熟人名单一样长。因此，我只能着重提及少数几位对我影响至深的人，即便记忆有误，他们的影响也难以完全抹去。

The autobiographical fragments with which this preface opens will serve to acknowledge what I can recognize of my main debt both to the works of scholarship and to the institutions that have helped give form to my thought. The remainder of that debt I shall try to discharge by citation in the pages that follow. Nothing said above or below, however, will more than hint at the number and nature of my personal obligations to the many individuals whose suggestions and criticisms have at one time or another sustained and directed my intellectual development. Too much time has elapsed since the ideas in this essay began to take shape; a list of all those who may properly find some signs of their influence in its pages would be almost coextensive with a list of my friends and acquaintances. Under the circumstances, I must restrict myself to the few most significant influences that even a faulty memory will never entirely suppress.

是时任哈佛大学校长的詹姆斯·B·康南特先生，他首先将我引入科学史领域，从而开启了我对科学进步本质认知的转变。自此之后，他一直慷慨地分享他的想法、批评和时间——包括阅读我的手稿草稿并提出重要修改意见。伦纳德·K·纳什先生，我曾与他共同教授康南特博士创办的这门以历史为导向的课程长达五年之久，在我最初构思的那些年里，他是一位更为积极的合作者，而在我的思想发展后期，他的缺席令我倍感惋惜。幸运的是，在我离开剑桥之后，我的伯克利同事斯坦利·卡维尔先生接替了他作为创意顾问的角色，并发挥了更大的作用。卡维尔先生是一位主要关注伦理学和美学的哲学家，但他得出的结论却与我如此契合，这始终激励着我不断前行。此外，他也是我唯一一位能够与我用不完整句子探讨我的想法的人。这种沟通方式这证明他理解我的情况，使我能够指导我克服或绕过我在准备第一部手稿时遇到的几个主要障碍。

It was James B. Conant, then president of Harvard University, who first introduced me to the history of science and thus initiated the transformation in my conception of the nature of scientific advance. Ever since that process began, he has been generous of his ideas, criticisms, and time—including the time required to read and suggest important changes in the draft of my manuscript. Leonard K. Nash, with whom for five years I taught the historically oriented course that Dr. Conant had started, was an even more active collaborator during the years when my ideas first began to take shape, and he has been much missed during the later stages of their development. Fortunately, however, after my departure from Cambridge, his place as creative sounding board and more was assumed by my Berkeley colleague, Stanley Cavell. That Cavell, a philosopher mainly concerned with ethics and aesthetics, should have reached conclusions quite so congruent to my own has been a constant source of stimulation and encouragement to me. He is, furthermore, the only person with whom I have ever been able to explore my ideas in incomplete sentences. That mode of communication attests an understanding that has enabled him to point me the way through or around several major barriers encountered while preparing my first manuscript.

自初稿完成以来，许多其他朋友也参与了修改润色。我想，如果我只提及四位贡献最为深远和关键的朋友，他们应该会原谅我：伯克利的保罗·K·费耶阿本德、哥伦比亚的欧内斯特·纳格尔、劳伦斯辐射实验室的H·皮埃尔·诺伊斯，以及我的学生约翰·L·海尔布伦，他经常与我密切合作，共同准备最终的出版版本。我发现他们提出的所有意见和建议都极其有益，但我没有理由相信（而且我也有理由怀疑）他们或上述其他几位是否完全认可最终的稿件。

Since that version was drafted, many other friends have helped with its reformulation. They will, I think, forgive me if I name only the four whose contributions proved most far-reaching and decisive: Paul K. Feyerabend of Berkeley, Ernest Nagel of Columbia, H. Pierre Noyes of the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory, and my student, John L. Heilbron, who has often worked closely with me in preparing a final version for the press. I have found all their reservations and suggestions extremely helpful, but I have no reason to believe (and some reason to doubt) that either they or the others mentioned above approve in its entirety the manuscript that results.

最后，我要向我的父母、妻子和孩子们表达一种截然不同的感谢。或许我最后才会意识到，他们每个人都以某种方式为我的创作贡献了智慧。但他们也以不同的方式做了一件更重要的事：他们支持我的创作，甚至鼓励我全身心投入其中。任何曾为类似我这样的项目苦苦挣扎的人都会明白，这有时需要付出怎样的代价。我不知道该如何表达对他们的感激之情。

My final acknowledgments, to my parents, wife, and children, must be of a rather different sort. In ways which I shall probably be the last to recognize, each of them, too, has contributed intellectual ingredients to my work. But they have also, in varying degrees, done something more important. They have, that is, let it go on and even encouraged my devotion to it. Anyone who has wrestled with a project like mine will recognize what it has occasionally cost them. I do not know how to give them thanks.

TSK

T. S. K.

B ERKELEY，加利福尼亚州

BERKELEY, CALIFORNIA

1962年2月

February 1962

[我]

[I]

介绍

Introduction

历史的作用

A Role for History

如果将历史视为一个超越轶事或年表的宝库，它或许能够彻底改变我们如今对科学的认知。这种认知，即便科学家们自身，也主要来源于对已完成的科学成就的研究，这些成就记录在经典著作中，而近年来，则更多地出现在教科书中——每一代科学家都从这些教科书中学习实践。然而，这类书籍的目的必然是说服和教学性的；从中得出的科学概念，与产生这些概念的科学事业本身，并无比契合之处，正如从旅游手册或语言教材中得出的民族文化形象一样。本文试图指出，我们在根本上被这些书籍误导了。其目的是勾勒出一个截然不同的科学概念，这个概念可以从科研活动本身的历史记录中浮现出来。

History, if viewed as a repository for more than anecdote or chronology, could produce a decisive transformation in the image of science by which we are now possessed. That image has previously been drawn, even by scientists themselves, mainly from the study of finished scientific achievements as these are recorded in the classics and, more recently, in the textbooks from which each new scientific generation learns to practice its trade. Inevitably, however, the aim of such books is persuasive and pedagogic; a concept of science drawn from them is no more likely to fit the enterprise that produced them than an image of a national culture drawn from a tourist brochure or a language text. This essay attempts to show that we have been misled by them in fundamental ways. Its aim is a sketch of the quite different concept of science that can emerge from the historical record of the research activity itself.

然而，即便从历史角度来看，如果人们继续主要为了回答那些源自科学文本的非历史性刻板印象而寻求和审视历史数据，那么这种新概念也无法出现。例如，这些文本常常暗示，科学的内容只能通过其所描述的观察、定律和理论来体现。几乎同样常见的情况是，同样的几本书也被解读为：科学方法仅仅是指教科书中用来收集数据的操作技巧，以及将这些数据与教科书中的理论概括联系起来时所运用的逻辑运算。这种解读产生了一种对科学本质和发展有着深刻影响的科学观念。

Even from history, however, that new concept will not be forthcoming if historical data continue to be sought and scrutinized mainly to answer questions posed by the unhistorical stereotype drawn from science texts. Those texts have, for example, often seemed to imply that the content of science is uniquely exemplified by the observations, laws, and theories described in their pages. Almost as regularly, the same books have been read as saying that scientific methods are simply the ones illustrated by the manipulative techniques used in gathering textbook data, together with the logical operations employed when relating those data to the textbook’s theoretical generalizations. The result has been a concept of science with profound implications about its nature and development.

如果说科学是汇集于现有文献中的事实、理论和方法的集合，那么科学家就是那些无论成功与否，都致力于为这一集合贡献不同要素的人。科学发展是一个循序渐进的过程，在这个过程中，这些要素被单独或组合地添加到不断增长的科学技术和知识库中。而科学史则成为一门记录这些渐进增长以及阻碍其积累的障碍的学科。关注科学发展的历史学家似乎有两个主要任务。一方面，他必须确定每一项当代科学事实、定律和理论是由谁在何时发现或发明的。另一方面，他必须描述和解释阻碍现代科学文本构成要素快速积累的各种谬误、神话和迷信。许多研究都致力于实现这些目标，并且目前仍在进行中。

If science is the constellation of facts, theories, and methods collected in current texts, then scientists are the men who, successfully or not, have striven to contribute one or another element to that particular constellation. Scientific development becomes the piecemeal process by which these items have been added, singly and in combination, to the ever growing stockpile that constitutes scientific technique and knowledge. And history of science becomes the discipline that chronicles both these successive increments and the obstacles that have inhibited their accumulation. Concerned with scientific development, the historian then appears to have two main tasks. On the one hand, he must determine by what man and at what point in time each contemporary scientific fact, law, and theory was discovered or invented. On the other, he must describe and explain the congeries of error, myth, and superstition that have inhibited the more rapid accumulation of the constituents of the modern science text. Much research has been directed to these ends, and some still is.

然而，近年来，一些科学史学家发现，他们越来越难以履行“积累式发展”概念赋予他们的职责。作为渐进过程的记录者，他们发现，更多的研究反而使诸如“氧气何时被发现？”“谁最先提出了能量守恒？”之类的问题更难回答，而不是更容易回答。越来越多的人开始怀疑，这些问题本身就是错误的。或许科学的发展并非源于个体发现和发明的积累。与此同时，这些科学史学家也面临着越来越大的困难，即如何区分过去观察和信念中的“科学”成分，以及他们的前辈们轻易贴上“错误”和“迷信”标签的内容。他们越是仔细研究，例如亚里士多德动力学、燃素化学或热质说，就越会发现，科学史中那些被科学界视为“错误”和“迷信”的部分，与科学史本身之间的联系也越来越紧密。在热力学领域，人们越发确信，那些曾经流行的自然观，总体而言，既不比当今的自然观更缺乏科学性，也不比当今的自然观更受人类个人偏好的影响。如果将这些过时的信念称为神话，那么神话的产生方式和持有理由，与如今形成科学知识的方式并无二致。反之，如果将它们称为科学，那么科学就包含了与我们今天所持有的信念完全不相容的信仰体系。鉴于这两种选择，历史学家必须选择后者。过时的理论并非因为被摒弃就一定不科学。然而，这种选择使得我们难以将科学发展视为一个累积的过程。同样的历史研究揭示了将单个发明和发现孤立出来的困难，也使人们对这些科学贡献的累积过程产生了深刻的怀疑。

In recent years, however, a few historians of science have been finding it more and more difficult to fulfil the functions that the concept of development-by-accumulation assigns to them. As chroniclers of an incremental process, they discover that additional research makes it harder, not easier, to answer questions like: When was oxygen discovered? Who first conceived of energy conservation? Increasingly, a few of them suspect that these are simply the wrong sorts of questions to ask. Perhaps science does not develop by the accumulation of individual discoveries and inventions. Simultaneously, these same historians confront growing difficulties in distinguishing the “scientific” component of past observation and belief from what their predecessors had readily labeled “error” and “superstition.” The more carefully they study, say, Aristotelian dynamics, phlogistic chemistry, or caloric thermodynamics, the more certain they feel that those once current views of nature were, as a whole, neither less scientific nor more the product of human idiosyncrasy than those current today. If these out-of-date beliefs are to be called myths, then myths can be produced by the same sorts of methods and held for the same sorts of reasons that now lead to scientific knowledge. If, on the other hand, they are to be called science, then science has included bodies of belief quite incompatible with the ones we hold today. Given these alternatives, the historian must choose the latter. Out-of-date theories are not in principle unscientific because they have been discarded. That choice, however, makes it difficult to see scientific development as a process of accretion. The same historical research that displays the difficulties in isolating individual inventions and discoveries gives ground for profound doubts about the cumulative process through which these individual contributions to science were thought to have been compounded.

所有这些疑虑和困难最终促成了科学研究史学领域的一场革命，尽管这场革命仍处于起步阶段。科学史学家们逐渐地，往往在不知不觉中，开始提出新的问题，并追溯科学发展的不同路径，这些路径通常并非累积性的。他们不再寻求早期科学对我们今天视角的永久性贡献，而是试图展现该科学在其时代背景下的历史完整性。例如，他们关注的不是伽利略的观点与现代科学的观点之间的关系，而是他的观点与他所属群体（即他的老师、同时代人和科学领域的直接继承者）的观点之间的关系。此外，他们坚持从一种视角——通常与现代科学截然不同——来研究该群体及其他类似群体的观点，这种视角能够使这些观点具有最大的内在一致性，并尽可能地符合自然规律。从由此产生的作品来看，尤其是亚历山大·科伊雷的著作，科学似乎与旧史学传统中作家们所讨论的科学并非完全相同。至少从某种意义上说，这些历史研究暗示了一种新的科学图景的可能性。本文旨在通过明确阐述新史学的一些含义来描绘这一形象。

The result of all these doubts and difficulties is a historiographic revolution in the study of science, though one that is still in its early stages. Gradually, and often without entirely realizing they are doing so, historians of science have begun to ask new sorts of questions and to trace different, and often less than cumulative, developmental lines for the sciences. Rather than seeking the permanent contributions of an older science to our present vantage, they attempt to display the historical integrity of that science in its own time. They ask, for example, not about the relation of Galileo’s views to those of modern science, but rather about the relationship between his views and those of his group, i.e., his teachers, contemporaries, and immediate successors in the sciences. Furthermore, they insist upon studying the opinions of that group and other similar ones from the viewpoint—usually very different from that of modern science—that gives those opinions the maximum internal coherence and the closest possible fit to nature. Seen through the works that result, works perhaps best exemplified in the writings of Alexandre Koyré, science does not seem altogether the same enterprise as the one discussed by writers in the older historiographic tradition. By implication, at least, these historical studies suggest the possibility of a new image of science. This essay aims to delineate that image by making explicit some of the new historiography’s implications.

在此过程中，科学的哪些方面将脱颖而出？首先，至少就呈现顺序而言，是方法论指导本身不足以对许多科学问题给出唯一的实质性结论。如果让一个对这些领域一无所知但懂得科学的人去研究电学或化学现象，他可能会得出许多互不相容的结论。在这些合理的可能性中，他最终得出的具体结论很可能取决于他之前在其他领域的经验、研究过程中的偶然因素以及他自身的个人特质。例如，他对星辰的哪些信念会带入化学或电学的研究中？在众多与新领域相关的实验中，他会首先选择进行哪一项？而由此产生的复杂现象中，哪些方面让他觉得与阐明化学变化或电亲和力的本质尤为相关？至少对个人而言，有时对科学界而言也是如此，这类问题的答案往往是科学发展的关键决定因素。例如，我们将在第二部分指出，大多数科学的早期发展阶段都以多种不同的自然观之间的持续竞争为特征，每一种自然观都部分源于科学观察和方法的指导原则，并且大致与之相符。区分这些不同学派的并非某种方法上的缺陷——它们都是“科学的”——而是我们接下来要称之为它们看待世界和实践科学方式的不可通约之处。观察和经验能够也必须极大地限制可接受的科学信念的范围，否则科学便不复存在。但它们本身并不能决定某种特定的信念体系。在特定时期，特定科学界所秉持的信念中，始终存在着一个看似任意的因素，它是由个人和历史偶然性交织而成。

What aspects of science will emerge to prominence in the course of this effort? First, at least in order of presentation, is the insufficiency of methodological directives, by themselves, to dictate a unique substantive conclusion to many sorts of scientific questions. Instructed to examine electrical or chemical phenomena, the man who is ignorant of these fields but who knows what it is to be scientific may legitimately reach any one of a number of incompatible conclusions. Among those legitimate possibilities, the particular conclusions he does arrive at are probably determined by his prior experience in other fields, by the accidents of his investigation, and by his own individual makeup. What beliefs about the stars, for example, does he bring to the study of chemistry or electricity? Which of the many conceivable experiments relevant to the new field does he elect to perform first? And what aspects of the complex phenomenon that then results strike him as particularly relevant to an elucidation of the nature of chemical change or of electrical affinity? For the individual, at least, and sometimes for the scientific community as well, answers to questions like these are often essential determinants of scientific development. We shall note, for example, in Section II that the early developmental stages of most sciences have been characterized by continual competition between a number of distinct views of nature, each partially derived from, and all roughly compatible with, the dictates of scientific observation and method. What differentiated these various schools was not one or another failure of method—they were all “scientific”—but what we shall come to call their incommensurable ways of seeing the world and of practicing science in it. Observation and experience can and must drastically restrict the range of admissible scientific belief, else there would be no science. But they cannot alone determine a particular body of such belief. An apparently arbitrary element, compounded of personal and historical accident, is always a formative ingredient of the beliefs espoused by a given scientific community at a given time.

然而，这种任意性因素并不意味着任何科学团体无需遵循任何既定信念也能开展研究。但这并不意味着该团体在特定时期所秉持的特定信念体系就不重要。有效的科研活动往往始于科学共同体自认为已掌握了诸如以下问题的确切答案：宇宙的基本构成要素是什么？这些要素之间以及它们如何与感官相互作用？关于这些要素，哪些问题可以合理地提出？又该采用哪些技术来寻求答案？至少在成熟的科学领域，这些问题的答案（或答案的完全替代方案）已牢牢地融入到培养学生专业实践能力的教育体系中。由于这种教育既严谨又僵化，这些答案便深深地烙印在科学家的思维之中。正是由于这些答案的影响力，才使得常规科研活动拥有如此卓越的效率，并决定了其在任何特定时期的发展方向。在第三、四、五部分探讨常规科学时，我们最终会将这类研究描述为一种艰苦卓绝的尝试，即试图将自然界纳入专业教育所提供的概念框架之中。与此同时，我们也会思考，无论这些框架的历史起源以及其后续发展中偶尔存在的任意性因素如何，研究是否还能脱离这些框架而继续进行。

That element of arbitrariness does not, however, indicate that any scientific group could practice its trade without some set of received beliefs. Nor does it make less consequential the particular constellation to which the group, at a given time, is in fact committed. Effective research scarcely begins before a scientific community thinks it has acquired firm answers to questions like the following: What are the fundamental entities of which the universe is composed? How do these interact with each other and with the senses? What questions may legitimately be asked about such entities and what techniques employed in seeking solutions? At least in the mature sciences, answers (or full substitutes for answers) to questions like these are firmly embedded in the educational initiation that prepares and licenses the student for professional practice. Because that education is both rigorous and rigid, these answers come to exert a deep hold on the scientific mind. That they can do so does much to account both for the peculiar efficiency of the normal research activity and for the direction in which it proceeds at any given time. When examining normal science in Sections III, IV, and V, we shall want finally to describe that research as a strenuous and devoted attempt to force nature into the conceptual boxes supplied by professional education. Simultaneously, we shall wonder whether research could proceed without such boxes, whatever the element of arbitrariness in their historic origins and, occasionally, in their subsequent development.

然而，这种任意性因素确实存在，并且它也对科学发展产生重要影响，这一点将在第六、七、八节中详细探讨。常规科学，即大多数科学家不可避免地将几乎所有时间投入其中的活动，其前提假设是科学界了解世界的本来面目。这项事业的成功很大程度上源于科学界愿意捍卫这一假设，即使这意味着要付出相当大的代价。例如，常规科学常常压制一些根本性的创新，因为它们必然会颠覆其基本承诺。然而，只要这些承诺保留着一定程度的任意性，常规研究的本质就保证了创新不会被长期压制。有时，一个看似正常的、应该可以用已知规则解决的问题，常规科学程序，会抵挡住其所属能力范围内最杰出成员的反复挑战。有时，为常规研究而设计和制造的设备无法按预期运行，揭示出一种异常现象，这种异常现象即便反复努力也无法与专业预期相符。在这些以及其他方面，常规科学屡屡误入歧途。而当这种情况发生时——也就是说，当该行业再也无法回避那些颠覆现有科学实践传统的异常现象时——就会展开非凡的调查，最终引导该行业走向一套新的承诺，一个全新的科学实践基础。本文将这种专业承诺转变发生的非凡事件称为科学革命。它们是打破传统的补充，是对常规科学活动的一种颠覆性补充。

Yet that element of arbitrariness is present, and it too has an important effect on scientific development, one which will be examined in detail in Sections VI, VII, and VIII. Normal science, the activity in which most scientists inevitably spend almost all their time, is predicated on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like. Much of the success of the enterprise derives from the community’s willingness to defend that assumption, if necessary at considerable cost. Normal science, for example, often suppresses fundamental novelties because they are necessarily subversive of its basic commitments. Nevertheless, so long as those commitments retain an element of the arbitrary, the very nature of normal research ensures that novelty shall not be suppressed for very long. Sometimes a normal problem, one that ought to be solvable by known rules and procedures, resists the reiterated onslaught of the ablest members of the group within whose competence it falls. On other occasions a piece of equipment designed and constructed for the purpose of normal research fails to perform in the anticipated manner, revealing an anomaly that cannot, despite repeated effort, be aligned with professional expectation. In these and other ways besides, normal science repeatedly goes astray. And when it does—when, that is, the profession can no longer evade anomalies that subvert the existing tradition of scientific practice—then begin the extraordinary investigations that lead the profession at last to a new set of commitments, a new basis for the practice of science. The extraordinary episodes in which that shift of professional commitments occurs are the ones known in this essay as scientific revolutions. They are the tradition-shattering complements to the tradition-bound activity of normal science.

科学革命最显而易见的例子莫过于那些在科学发展史上常被冠以“革命”之名的著名事件。因此，在第九节和第十节中，我们将首次直接审视科学革命的本质，并反复探讨与哥白尼、牛顿、拉瓦锡和爱因斯坦的名字相关的科学发展重大转折点。至少在物理科学史上，这些事件比大多数其他事件更清晰地展现了所有科学革命的本质。每一次革命都迫使科学界摒弃一种由来已久的科学理论，转而接受另一种与之不相容的理论。每一次革命都导致了可供科学研究的问题范围以及科学界判断何为可接受的问题或合法问题解决方案的标准发生相应的转变。每一次革命都从根本上改变了科学的想象力，而这种转变最终需要被描述为对科学工作所处世界的变革。这些变化，以及几乎总是伴随而来的争议，是科学革命的显著特征。

The most obvious examples of scientific revolutions are those famous episodes in scientific development that have often been labeled revolutions before. Therefore, in Sections IX and X, where the nature of scientific revolutions is first directly scrutinized, we shall deal repeatedly with the major turning points in scientific development associated with the names of Copernicus, Newton, Lavoisier, and Einstein. More clearly than most other episodes in the history of at least the physical sciences, these display what all scientific revolutions are about. Each of them necessitated the community’s rejection of one time-honored scientific theory in favor of another incompatible with it. Each produced a consequent shift in the problems available for scientific scrutiny and in the standards by which the profession determined what should count as an admissible problem or as a legitimate problem-solution. And each transformed the scientific imagination in ways that we shall ultimately need to describe as a transformation of the world within which scientific work was done. Such changes, together with the controversies that almost always accompany them, are the defining characteristics of scientific revolutions.

这些特征在对牛顿力学或化学革命等的研究中体现得尤为清晰。然而，本文的一个基本论点是，这些特征也可以从其他领域获得。对许多其他并不那么显而易见具有革命性的事件的研究。对于受其影响的规模小得多的专业群体而言，麦克斯韦方程组与爱因斯坦的方程组一样具有革命性，因此也遭到了抵制。其他新理论的出现，通常也会在与其专业领域相关的专家群体中引发同样的反应，这无可厚非。对这些人来说，新理论意味着对既有科学实践规则的改变。因此，它不可避免地会影响到他们已经成功完成的许多科学工作。这就是为什么一个新理论，无论其应用范围多么特殊，都很少或几乎不可能仅仅是对已知知识的补充。它的吸收需要重构先前的理论并重新评估先前的事实，这是一个本质上具有革命性的过程，很少能由一个人完成，也绝不可能在一夜之间完成。难怪历史学家很难准确地确定这一漫长过程的确切时间，因为他们的词汇习惯于将其视为一个孤立事件。

These characteristics emerge with particular clarity from a study of, say, the Newtonian or the chemical revolution. It is, however, a fundamental thesis of this essay that they can also be retrieved from the study of many other episodes that were not so obviously revolutionary. For the far smaller professional group affected by them, Maxwell’s equations were as revolutionary as Einstein’s, and they were resisted accordingly. The invention of other new theories regularly, and appropriately, evokes the same response from some of the specialists on whose area of special competence they impinge. For these men the new theory implies a change in the rules governing the prior practice of normal science. Inevitably, therefore, it reflects upon much scientific work they have already successfully completed. That is why a new theory, however special its range of application, is seldom or never just an increment to what is already known. Its assimilation requires the reconstruction of prior theory and the re-evaluation of prior fact, an intrinsically revolutionary process that is seldom completed by a single man and never overnight. No wonder historians have had difficulty in dating precisely this extended process that their vocabulary impels them to view as an isolated event.

理论的新发明并非唯一对相关领域专家产生革命性影响的科学事件。支配常规科学的原则不仅明确了宇宙包含哪些实体，也间接地明确了宇宙不包含哪些实体。由此可见（尽管这一点需要进一步探讨），像氧气或X射线这样的发现并非仅仅是为科学家的世界增添了一项新成员。最终，它们确实会产生这种影响，但这只有在专业界重新评估了传统的实验程序，改变了其长期以来熟悉的实体概念，并在这一过程中转变了其赖以理解世界的理论网络之后才会发生。科学事实和理论并非截然分开，或许只有在单一的常规科学实践传统中才能如此。正因如此，意外发现的意义不仅仅在于事实层面，也正因事实或理论的根本性创新，科学家的世界才会在数量上得到丰富，而在质量上得到转变。

Nor are new inventions of theory the only scientific events that have revolutionary impact upon the specialists in whose domain they occur. The commitments that govern normal science specify not only what sorts of entities the universe does contain, but also, by implication, those that it does not. It follows, though the point will require extended discussion, that a discovery like that of oxygen or X-rays does not simply add one more item to the population of the scientist’s world. Ultimately it has that effect, but not until the professional community has re-evaluated traditional experimental procedures, altered its conception of entities with which it has long been familiar, and, in the process, shifted the network of theory through which it deals with the world. Scientific fact and theory are not categorically separable, except perhaps within a single tradition of normal-scientific practice. That is why the unexpected discovery is not simply factual in its import and why the scientist’s world is qualitatively transformed as well as quantitatively enriched by fundamental novelties of either fact or theory.

接下来的篇幅将详细阐述这种对科学革命本质的扩展概念。诚然，这种扩展概念本身也是一种扩展。这与惯常用法有所出入。尽管如此，我仍将把发现称为革命性的，因为正是将它们的结构与例如哥白尼革命的结构联系起来的可能性，才使得这种扩展的概念在我看来如此重要。前面的讨论表明，接下来的九个章节将如何发展常规科学和科学革命这两个互补的概念。本文的其余部分试图解决三个剩余的核心问题。第十一节通过讨论教科书传统，探讨了为什么科学革命此前如此难以被察觉。第十二节描述了旧常规科学传统的支持者和新传统拥护者之间的革命性竞争。由此，它探讨了在科学探究理论中，应该以某种方式取代我们通常所熟悉的科学认知中常见的证实或证伪程序的过程。科学界不同群体之间的竞争是唯一真正导致先前被接受的理论被否定或被另一种理论采纳的历史进程。最后，第十三节将探讨通过革命实现的发展如何能够与科学进步看似独特的性质相兼容。然而，对于这个问题，本文只能提供答案的主要轮廓，而答案取决于科学界的特征，这需要进一步的探索和研究。

This extended conception of the nature of scientific revolutions is the one delineated in the pages that follow. Admittedly the extension strains customary usage. Nevertheless, I shall continue to speak even of discoveries as revolutionary, because it is just the possibility of relating their structure to that of, say, the Copernican revolution that makes the extended conception seem to me so important. The preceding discussion indicates how the complementary notions of normal science and of scientific revolutions will be developed in the nine sections immediately to follow. The rest of the essay attempts to dispose of three remaining central questions. Section XI, by discussing the textbook tradition, considers why scientific revolutions have previously been so difficult to see. Section XII describes the revolutionary competition between the proponents of the old normal-scientific tradition and the adherents of the new one. It thus considers the process that should somehow, in a theory of scientific inquiry, replace the confirmation or falsification procedures made familiar by our usual image of science. Competition between segments of the scientific community is the only historical process that ever actually results in the rejection of one previously accepted theory or in the adoption of another. Finally, Section XIII will ask how development through revolutions can be compatible with the apparently unique character of scientific progress. For that question, however, this essay will provide no more than the main outlines of an answer, one which depends upon characteristics of the scientific community that require much additional exploration and study.

毫无疑问，一些读者或许已经质疑，历史研究是否能够实现本文旨在探讨的那种概念转变。种种二元对立的论证似乎都表明历史研究无法做到这一点。我们常常说，历史是一门纯粹的描述性学科。然而，上文提出的论点往往具有解释性，有时也具有规范性。此外，我的许多概括都与科学家的社会学或社会心理学相关；然而，我的结论中至少有一些传统上属于逻辑学或认识论的范畴。在前一段中，我甚至可能似乎违反了当代颇具影响力的“发现的语境”与“论证的语境”之间的区分。除了……之外，还有什么能比这更进一步呢？这种不同领域和问题的混杂是否表明存在严重的混乱？

Undoubtedly, some readers will already have wondered whether historical study can possibly effect the sort of conceptual transformation aimed at here. An entire arsenal of dichotomies is available to suggest that it cannot properly do so. History, we too often say, is a purely descriptive discipline. The theses suggested above are, however, often interpretive and sometimes normative. Again, many of my generalizations are about the sociology or social psychology of scientists; yet at least a few of my conclusions belong traditionally to logic or epistemology. In the preceding paragraph I may even seem to have violated the very influential contemporary distinction between “the context of discovery” and “the context of justification.” Can anything more than profound confusion be indicated by this admixture of diverse fields and concerns?

我从小就接受这些区分以及其他类似区分的熏陶，因此我几乎无法更深刻地意识到它们的重要性和力量。多年来，我一直认为它们关乎知识的本质，而且我仍然认为，如果加以适当的重新阐释，它们确实蕴含着重要的启示。然而，我尝试将它们应用到知识获取、接受和吸收的实际情境中，哪怕只是粗略地应用，也使它们显得异常棘手。它们不再是基本的逻辑或方法论区分（因此它们应该先于科学知识的分析），而是成为了传统实质性答案体系的组成部分，而这些答案恰恰是它们所针对的问题。这种循环论证丝毫不会否定它们。但这确实使它们成为某种理论的一部分，并因此使它们受到与其他领域理论相同的审视。如果它们的内容不仅仅是纯粹的抽象概念，那么就必须通过观察它们在实际应用于它们旨在阐明的数据时的表现来发现其内容。科学史怎么可能不是知识理论可以合理应用于的现象的来源呢？

Having been weaned intellectually on these distinctions and others like them, I could scarcely be more aware of their import and force. For many years I took them to be about the nature of knowledge, and I still suppose that, appropriately recast, they have something important to tell us. Yet my attempts to apply them, even grosso modo, to the actual situations in which knowledge is gained, accepted, and assimilated have made them seem extraordinarily problematic. Rather than being elementary logical or methodological distinctions, which would thus be prior to the analysis of scientific knowledge, they now seem integral parts of a traditional set of substantive answers to the very questions upon which they have been deployed. That circularity does not at all invalidate them. But it does make them parts of a theory and, by doing so, subjects them to the same scrutiny regularly applied to theories in other fields. If they are to have more than pure abstraction as their content, then that content must be discovered by observing them in application to the data they are meant to elucidate. How could history of science fail to be a source of phenomena to which theories about knowledge may legitimately be asked to apply?

[ II ]

[II]

通往正常科学之路

The Route to Normal Science

本文中，“常规科学”指的是以一项或多项过去的科学成就为基础的研究，这些成就曾被某些特定的科学共同体认可，并被其视为未来实践的基石。如今，无论是初级还是高级科学教科书，都会对这些成就进行叙述，尽管很少以其原始形式呈现。这些教科书阐述了公认的理论体系，展示了其众多或全部的成功应用，并将这些应用与典型的观察和实验进行比较。在十九世纪初这类书籍流行之前（甚至在近期新兴的科学领域也是如此），许多著名的科学经典都发挥着类似的作用。亚里士多德的《物理学》、托勒密的《天文学大成》、牛顿的《自然哲学的数学原理》和《光学》、富兰克林的《电学》、拉瓦锡的《化学》以及莱伊尔的《地质学》 ——这些著作以及其他许多著作，都曾在一段时间内隐晦地为后世的实践者界定了某个研究领域的合法问题和方法。它们之所以能够做到这一点，是因为它们具有两个基本特征。他们的成就前所未有，足以吸引一批忠实的追随者，使他们远离其他科学活动模式。与此同时，它也……足够开放，可以给重新定义的从业者群体留下各种各样的问题来解决。

In this essay, ‘normal science’ means research firmly based upon one or more past scientific achievements, achievements that some particular scientific community acknowledges for a time as supplying the foundation for its further practice. Today such achievements are recounted, though seldom in their original form, by science textbooks, elementary and advanced. These textbooks expound the body of accepted theory, illustrate many or all of its successful applications, and compare these applications with exemplary observations and experiments. Before such books became popular early in the nineteenth century (and until even more recently in the newly matured sciences), many of the famous classics of science fulfilled a similar function. Aristotle’s Physica, Ptolemy’s Almagest, Newton’s Principia and Opticks, Franklin’s Electricity, Lavoisier’s Chemistry, and Lyell’s Geology—these and many other works served for a time implicitly to define the legitimate problems and methods of a research field for succeeding generations of practitioners. They were able to do so because they shared two essential characteristics. Their achievement was sufficiently unprecedented to attract an enduring group of adherents away from competing modes of scientific activity. Simultaneously, it was sufficiently open-ended to leave all sorts of problems for the redefined group of practitioners to resolve.

我将具备上述两个特征的成就称为“范式”，这个术语与“常规科学”密切相关。我之所以选择这个词，是想表明一些公认的实际科学实践案例——这些案例包含了规律、理论、应用和仪器——为特定的、连贯的科学研究传统提供了模型。这些传统正是历史学家用“托勒密天文学”（或“哥白尼天文学”）、“亚里士多德动力学”（或“牛顿动力学”）、“微粒光学”（或“波动光学”）等术语来描述的。对范式的研究，包括许多比上述例子更为专业的范式，是学生为日后加入特定科学共同体做好准备的主要途径。因为他将与那些从相同的具体模型中学习了各自领域基础的人们一起，所以他日后的实践很少会引发关于基本原理的公开争论。基于共同范式进行研究的学者，都恪守相同的科学实践规则和标准。这种恪守以及由此产生的共识，是正常科学的先决条件，即特定研究传统的产生和延续的先决条件。

Achievements that share these two characteristics I shall henceforth refer to as ‘paradigms,’ a term that relates closely to ‘normal science.’ By choosing it, I mean to suggest that some accepted examples of actual scientific practice—examples which include law, theory, application, and instrumentation together—provide models from which spring particular coherent traditions of scientific research. These are the traditions which the historian describes under such rubrics as ‘Ptolemaic astronomy’ (or ‘Copernican’), ‘Aristotelian dynamics’ (or ‘Newtonian’), ‘corpuscular optics’ (or ‘wave optics’), and so on. The study of paradigms, including many that are far more specialized than those named illustratively above, is what mainly prepares the student for membership in the particular scientific community with which he will later practice. Because he there joins men who learned the bases of their field from the same concrete models, his subsequent practice will seldom evoke overt disagreement over fundamentals. Men whose research is based on shared paradigms are committed to the same rules and standards for scientific practice. That commitment and the apparent consensus it produces are prerequisites for normal science, i.e., for the genesis and continuation of a particular research tradition.

由于本文中“范式”概念将经常用来替代各种常见的概念，因此有必要进一步阐述引入该概念的原因。为什么具体的科学成就，作为专业承诺的体现，先于从中抽象出的各种概念、定律、理论和观点？对于研究科学发展的学生而言，共享的范式在何种意义上是一个基本单元？这个单元无法被完全还原为逻辑上可以替代它的原子性组成部分。当我们在第五部分遇到这些问题时，这些问题以及其他类似问题的答案对于理解常规科学和相关的范式概念都至关重要。然而，这种更为抽象的讨论将取决于读者事先接触过常规科学或范式运作的实例。特别是，通过指出存在一种无需范式，或者至少无需像上述范式那样明确且具有约束力的科学研究，可以阐明这两个相关概念。获得某种范式以及由此允许的更为深奥的研究类型，是任何特定科学领域发展成熟的标志。

Because in this essay the concept of a paradigm will often substitute for a variety of familiar notions, more will need to be said about the reasons for its introduction. Why is the concrete scientific achievement, as a locus of professional commitment, prior to the various concepts, laws, theories, and points of view that may be abstracted from it? In what sense is the shared paradigm a fundamental unit for the student of scientific development, a unit that cannot be fully reduced to logically atomic components which might function in its stead? When we encounter them in Section V, answers to these questions and to others like them will prove basic to an understanding both of normal science and of the associated concept of paradigms. That more abstract discussion will depend, however, upon a previous exposure to examples of normal science or of paradigms in operation. In particular, both these related concepts will be clarified by noting that there can be a sort of scientific research without paradigms, or at least without any so unequivocal and so binding as the ones named above. Acquisition of a paradigm and of the more esoteric type of research it permits is a sign of maturity in the development of any given scientific field.

如果历史学家追溯任何一组相关现象的科学知识发展历程，他很可能会遇到某种模式的细微变体，本文以物理光学史为例进行说明。如今的物理教科书告诉学生，光是光子，即兼具波和粒子特性的量子力学实体。研究也据此展开，或者更确切地说，是根据更为精细的数学表征进行，而这种表征正是我们通常所理解的。然而，这种对光的表征不过半个世纪的历史。在本世纪初普朗克、爱因斯坦等人提出这一理论之前，物理教科书一直认为光是横波运动，这一概念源于19世纪初杨和菲涅耳的光学著作。波动理论也并非几乎所有光学从业者都接受的第一个理论。18世纪，牛顿的《光学》为这一领域提供了范式，它认为光是物质微粒。当时，物理学家们寻求证据，以证明光粒子撞击固体时会产生压力，而早期的波动理论家们却没有这样做。1

If the historian traces the scientific knowledge of any selected group of related phenomena backward in time, he is likely to encounter some minor variant of a pattern here illustrated from the history of physical optics. Today’s physics textbooks tell the student that light is photons, i.e., quantum-mechanical entities that exhibit some characteristics of waves and some of particles. Research proceeds accordingly, or rather according to the more elaborate and mathematical characterization from which this usual verbalization is derived. That characterization of light is, however, scarcely half a century old. Before it was developed by Planck, Einstein, and others early in this century, physics texts taught that light was transverse wave motion, a conception rooted in a paradigm that derived ultimately from the optical writings of Young and Fresnel in the early nineteenth century. Nor was the wave theory the first to be embraced by almost all practitioners of optical science. During the eighteenth century the paradigm for this field was provided by Newton’s Opticks, which taught that light was material corpuscles. At that time physicists sought evidence, as the early wave theorists had not, of the pressure exerted by light particles impinging on solid bodies.1

这些物理光学范式的转变是科学革命，而通过革命从一个范式逐步过渡到另一个范式，是成熟科学通常的发展模式。然而，这并非牛顿工作之前的时期所特有的模式，而这正是我们在此关注的对比。从远古时期到十七世纪末，没有任何时期出现过一种普遍接受的关于物理光学的单一观点。光的本质。然而，当时存在着许多相互竞争的学派和分支学派，它们大多信奉伊壁鸠鲁、亚里士多德或柏拉图理论的某种变体。有的学派认为光是从物质物体发出的粒子；有的学派则认为光是物体与眼睛之间介质的一种变化；还有的学派则从眼睛发出的光线与介质相互作用的角度来解释光；此外还有其他一些组合和变体。每个学派都从其与某种特定形而上学的联系中汲取力量，并且每个学派都强调其理论最能解释的特定光学现象群作为典型观察结果。其他观察结果则通过临时性的阐述来处理，或者作为有待进一步研究的悬而未决的问题而存在。2

These transformations of the paradigms of physical optics are scientific revolutions, and the successive transition from one paradigm to another via revolution is the usual developmental pattern of mature science. It is not, however, the pattern characteristic of the period before Newton’s work, and that is the contrast that concerns us here. No period between remote antiquity and the end of the seventeenth century exhibited a single generally accepted view about the nature of light. Instead there were a number of competing schools and subschools, most of them espousing one variant or another of Epicurean, Aristotelian, or Platonic theory. One group took light to be particles emanating from material bodies; for another it was a modification of the medium that intervened between the body and the eye; still another explained light in terms of an interaction of the medium with an emanation from the eye; and there were other combinations and modifications besides. Each of the corresponding schools derived strength from its relation to some particular metaphysic, and each emphasized, as paradigmatic observations, the particular cluster of optical phenomena that its own theory could do most to explain. Other observations were dealt with by ad hoc elaborations, or they remained as outstanding problems for further research.2

在不同的时期，所有这些学派都对概念、现象和技术体系做出了重要贡献，牛顿正是从中汲取灵感，构建了第一个几乎被普遍接受的物理光学范式。任何对科学家的定义，如果排除了这些学派中至少那些更具创造力的成员，那么也必然会排除他们的现代后继者。这些人都是科学家。然而，任何研究牛顿之前物理光学发展历程的人都可能得出这样的结论：尽管该领域的实践者是科学家，但他们活动的最终成果却远非科学。由于无法想当然地接受任何共同的信念体系，每一位物理光学学者都感到不得不从零开始重建自己的领域。正因如此，他们选择支持性观察和实验的相对自由，因为并没有一套标准的方法或现象是每位光学学者都必须采用和解释的。在这种情况下，最终形成的著作的对话对象往往既包括其他学派的成员，也包括自然本身。这种模式在当今许多创造性领域中并不罕见，而且也并非与重大发现和发明相悖。然而，这并不是牛顿之后物理光学所采用的发展模式，也不是我们今天所熟悉的其他自然科学的发展模式。

At various times all these schools made significant contributions to the body of concepts, phenomena, and techniques from which Newton drew the first nearly uniformly accepted paradigm for physical optics. Any definition of the scientist that excludes at least the more creative members of these various schools will exclude their modern successors as well. Those men were scientists. Yet anyone examining a survey of physical optics before Newton may well conclude that, though the field’s practitioners were scientists, the net result of their activity was something less than science. Being able to take no common body of belief for granted, each writer on physical optics felt forced to build his field anew from its foundations. In doing so, his choice of supporting observation and experiment was relatively free, for there was no standard set of methods or of phenomena that every optical writer felt forced to employ and explain. Under these circumstances, the dialogue of the resulting books was often directed as much to the members of other schools as it was to nature. That pattern is not unfamiliar in a number of creative fields today, nor is it incompatible with significant discovery and invention. It is not, however, the pattern of development that physical optics acquired after Newton and that other natural sciences make familiar today.

十八世纪上半叶的电学研究史提供了一个更为具体、更为人熟知的例子，展现了一门科学在获得其第一个被普遍接受的范式之前是如何发展的。在那段时期，关于电的本质的观点几乎与重要的电学实验者一样多，例如豪克斯比、格雷、德萨古利耶、杜菲、诺莱特、沃森、富兰克林等等。他们众多的电学概念有一个共同点——它们都部分源于当时指导所有科学研究的机械微粒论哲学的不同版本。此外，所有这些概念都是真实科学理论的组成部分，这些理论部分源于实验和观察，并在一定程度上决定了研究中其他问题的选择和解释。然而，尽管所有实验都与电学相关，而且大多数实验者都阅读过彼此的著作，但他们的理论却只有相似之处。3

The history of electrical research in the first half of the eighteenth century provides a more concrete and better known example of the way a science develops before it acquires its first universally received paradigm. During that period there were almost as many views about the nature of electricity as there were important electrical experimenters, men like Hauksbee, Gray, Desaguliers, Du Fay, Nollett, Watson, Franklin, and others. All their numerous concepts of electricity had something in common—they were partially derived from one or another version of the mechanico-corpuscular philosophy that guided all scientific research of the day. In addition, all were components of real scientific theories, of theories that had been drawn in part from experiment and observation and that partially determined the choice and interpretation of additional problems undertaken in research. Yet though all the experiments were electrical and though most of the experimenters read each other’s works, their theories had no more than a family resemblance.3

早期的一类理论，沿袭十七世纪的做法，将吸引和摩擦生热视为基本的电现象。​​这类理论倾向于将排斥视为某种机械反弹导致的次要效应，并尽可能推迟对格雷新发现的电导效应的讨论和系统研究。其他一些“电学家”（这个称谓是他们自己创造的）则认为吸引和排斥同样是电的基本表现形式，并据此修正了他们的理论和研究。（实际上，这类理论的作者人数非常少——即使是富兰克林的理论也从未完全解释过相互吸引和排斥的现象。）（例如两个带负电的物体之间的排斥力。）但他们和第一组人一样，难以同时解释除最简单的传导效应之外的任何其他效应。然而，这些效应为第三组人提供了起点，他们倾向于将电描述为一种可以在导体中流动的“流体”，而不是从非导体中散发出来的“逸散物”。反过来，这组人也难以将他们的理论与许多吸引和排斥效应调和起来。只有通过富兰克林及其直接后继者的工作，才出现了一种理论，能够以几乎相同的方式解释几乎所有这些效应，因此能够并且确实为后来的“电学家”提供了一个共同的研究范式。

One early group of theories, following seventeenth-century practice, regarded attraction and frictional generation as the fundamental electrical phenomena. This group tended to treat repulsion as a secondary effect due to some sort of mechanical rebounding and also to postpone for as long as possible both discussion and systematic research on Gray’s newly discovered effect, electrical conduction. Other “electricians” (the term is their own) took attraction and repulsion to be equally elementary manifestations of electricity and modified their theories and research accordingly. (Actually, this group is remarkably small—even Franklin’s theory never quite accounted for the mutual repulsion of two negatively charged bodies.) But they had as much difficulty as the first group in accounting simultaneously for any but the simplest conduction effects. Those effects, however, provided the starting point for still a third group, one which tended to speak of electricity as a “fluid” that could run through conductors rather than as an “effluvium” that emanated from non-conductors. This group, in its turn, had difficulty reconciling its theory with a number of attractive and repulsive effects. Only through the work of Franklin and his immediate successors did a theory arise that could account with something like equal facility for very nearly all these effects and that therefore could and did provide a subsequent generation of “electricians” with a common paradigm for its research.

撇开那些最早确立范式可追溯至史前时期的领域（如数学和天文学），以及那些由成熟学科分化重组而形成的领域（如生物化学），上述情况在历史上具有典型性。尽管这意味着我仍然沿用一种不幸的简化方法，即用一个单一且略显随意选择的名字（例如牛顿或富兰克林）来标记一段漫长的历史时期，但我认为，类似的根本性分歧也存在于其他领域，例如亚里士多德之前的运动学研究、阿基米德之前的静力学研究、布莱克之前的热学研究、波义耳和布尔哈夫之前的化学研究，以及赫顿之前的历史地质学研究。在生物学的某些领域——例如遗传学研究——第一个被普遍接受的范式出现得更晚；而社会科学的哪些领域已经获得了这样的范式，仍然是一个悬而未决的问题。历史表明，达成稳固的研究共识之路异常艰辛。

Excluding those fields, like mathematics and astronomy, in which the first firm paradigms date from prehistory and also those, like biochemistry, that arose by division and recombination of specialties already matured, the situations outlined above are historically typical. Though it involves my continuing to employ the unfortunate simplification that tags an extended historical episode with a single and somewhat arbitrarily chosen name (e.g., Newton or Franklin), I suggest that similar fundamental disagreements characterized, for example, the study of motion before Aristotle and of statics before Archimedes, the study of heat before Black, of chemistry before Boyle and Boerhaave, and of historical geology before Hutton. In parts of biology—the study of heredity, for example—the first universally received paradigms are still more recent; and it remains an open question what parts of social science have yet acquired such paradigms at all. History suggests that the road to a firm research consensus is extraordinarily arduous.

然而，历史也揭示了这条道路上所遭遇的种种困难的一些原因。在缺乏范式或范式候选者的情况下，所有可能与特定科学发展相关的事实都可能显得同等重要。因此，早期的事实收集活动远比后来科学发展所展现的那种随机性活动更为显著。此外，由于缺乏寻求某种特定深奥信息的理由，早期的事实收集通常会受到限制。触手可及的大量数据。由此产生的资料库既包含可通过日常观察和实验获取的信息，也包含一些可从传统技艺（如医学、历法制作和冶金）中获取的更为深奥的数据。由于这些技艺是获取难以偶然发现的事实的便捷途径之一，因此技术在新兴科学的出现过程中往往发挥了至关重要的作用。

History also suggests, however, some reasons for the difficulties encountered on that road. In the absence of a paradigm or some candidate for paradigm, all of the facts that could possibly pertain to the development of a given science are likely to seem equally relevant. As a result, early fact-gathering is a far more nearly random activity than the one that subsequent scientific development makes familiar. Furthermore, in the absence of a reason for seeking some particular form of more recondite information, early fact-gathering is usually restricted to the wealth of data that lie ready to hand. The resulting pool of facts contains those accessible to casual observation and experiment together with some of the more esoteric data retrievable from established crafts like medicine, calendar making, and metallurgy. Because the crafts are one readily accessible source of facts that could not have been casually discovered, technology has often played a vital role in the emergence of new sciences.

尽管这种事实收集对于许多重要科学的起源至关重要，但任何研究过普林尼的百科全书式著作或17世纪培根的自然史的人都会发现，它最终会造成混乱。人们很难将由此产生的文献称为科学文献。培根关于热、颜色、风、采矿等等的“历史”充满了信息，其中一些晦涩难懂。但它们将一些后来被证明具有启发性的事实（例如，混合加热）与另一些事实（例如，粪堆的温度）并列在一起，而后者在一段时间内仍然过于复杂，根本无法与理论整合。4此外，由于任何描述都必然是不完整的，典型的自然史往往会在其大量的细节描述中省略那些后来被科学家视为重要启示的资料。例如，几乎所有早期关于电的“历史”都没有提到，谷壳被摩擦过的玻璃棒吸引后会再次弹开。这种效应似乎是机械性的，而非电性的。5此外，由于普通的史料收集者很少有时间或工具进行批判性思考，自然史著作常常将上述描述与其他描述并列，例如通过反蠕动（或冷却）实现的加热，而我们现在完全无法证实这些描述。6只有极少数情况下，例如在古代的静力学、动力学中，几何光学领域，在几乎没有预先建立的理论指导下收集到的事实，是否能够清晰地表达出足以产生第一个范式的观点？

But though this sort of fact-collecting has been essential to the origin of many significant sciences, anyone who examines, for example, Pliny’s encyclopedic writings or the Baconian natural histories of the seventeenth century will discover that it produces a morass. One somehow hesitates to call the literature that results scientific. The Baconian “histories” of heat, color, wind, mining, and so on, are filled with information, some of it recondite. But they juxtapose facts that will later prove revealing (e.g., heating by mixture) with others (e.g., the warmth of dung heaps) that will for some time remain too complex to be integrated with theory at all.4 In addition, since any description must be partial, the typical natural history often omits from its immensely circumstantial accounts just those details that later scientists will find sources of important illumination. Almost none of the early “histories” of electricity, for example, mention that chaff, attracted to a rubbed glass rod, bounces off again. That effect seemed mechanical, not electrical.5 Moreover, since the casual fact-gatherer seldom possesses the time or the tools to be critical, the natural histories often juxtapose descriptions like the above with others, say, heating by antiperistasis (or by cooling), that we are now quite unable to confirm.6 Only very occasionally, as in the cases of ancient statics, dynamics, and geometrical optics, do facts collected with so little guidance from pre-established theory speak with sufficient clarity to permit the emergence of a first paradigm.

正是这种情况造就了科学发展早期阶段特有的学派。任何自然史的解读都离不开至少某种隐含的、相互交织的理论和方法论信念体系，这种体系允许进行选择、评估和批判。如果这种信念体系并非隐含于事实集合之中——在这种情况下，我们所拥有的就不仅仅是“事实”——那么它就必须从外部补充，或许来自当时的形而上学，或许来自其他科学，或许来自个人或历史的偶然事件。因此，任何科学发展的早期阶段，不同的人面对相同的现象（通常并非完全相同的具体现象），会以不同的方式描述和解释它们，也就不足为奇了。令人惊讶的是，或许也是我们称之为科学的领域中独有的现象，这种最初的分歧最终竟然会基本消失。

This is the situation that creates the schools characteristic of the early stages of a science’s development. No natural history can be interpreted in the absence of at least some implicit body of intertwined theoretical and methodological belief that permits selection, evaluation, and criticism. If that body of belief is not already implicit in the collection of facts—in which case more than “mere facts” are at hand—it must be externally supplied, perhaps by a current metaphysic, by another science, or by personal and historical accident. No wonder, then, that in the early stages of the development of any science different men confronting the same range of phenomena, but not usually all the same particular phenomena, describe and interpret them in different ways. What is surprising, and perhaps also unique in its degree to the fields we call science, is that such initial divergences should ever largely disappear.

因为它们确实会在很大程度上消失，而且似乎就此彻底消失。此外，它们的消失通常是由某个前范式学派的胜利造成的，这些学派由于自身特有的信念和先入之见，只强调了庞大而混沌的信息库中的某些特定部分。那些认为电是一种流体，因此特别强调导电性的电学家就是一个很好的例子。在这种信念的驱使下（这种信念几乎无法解释已知的各种吸引和排斥效应），他们中的一些人萌生了将这种“电流体”装瓶的想法。他们努力的直接成果是莱顿瓶，这种装置或许永远不会被一个随意或漫无目的地探索自然的人发现，但事实上，它至少是由两位研究者在18世纪40年代初独立研制出来的。7几乎从他开始进行电学研究之初，富兰克林就特别关注如何解释这种奇特的、最终却又极具启发性的特殊装置。他在这方面取得的成功，为他的理论成为典范提供了最有力的论据，尽管该理论仍然无法解释所有已知的电排斥现象。8一个理论要想被接受为典范，必须看起来优于其他竞争理论，但它无需，实际上也从未解释过所有与之相关的现象。

For they do disappear to a very considerable extent and then apparently once and for all. Furthermore, their disappearance is usually caused by the triumph of one of the pre-paradigm schools, which, because of its own characteristic beliefs and preconceptions, emphasized only some special part of the too sizable and inchoate pool of information. Those electricians who thought electricity a fluid and therefore gave particular emphasis to conduction provide an excellent case in point. Led by this belief, which could scarcely cope with the known multiplicity of attractive and repulsive effects, several of them conceived the idea of bottling the electrical fluid. The immediate fruit of their efforts was the Leyden jar, a device which might never have been discovered by a man exploring nature casually or at random, but which was in fact independently developed by at least two investigators in the early 1740’s.7 Almost from the start of his electrical researches, Franklin was particularly concerned to explain that strange and, in the event, particularly revealing piece of special apparatus. His success in doing so provided the most effective of the arguments that made his theory a paradigm, though one that was still unable to account for quite all the known cases of electrical repulsion.8 To be accepted as a paradigm, a theory must seem better than its competitors, but it need not, and in fact never does, explain all the facts with which it can be confronted.

流体电理论对持有该理论的小群体所产生的影响，后来被富兰克林范式所取代，后者对整个电学群体产生了同样的影响。它指明了哪些实验值得进行，哪些实验由于指向次要或过于复杂的电现象而显得不值得。只有这一范式才能更有效地完成这项工作，部分原因是学派间争论的结束终结了对基本原理的不断重复，部分原因是科学家们确信自己正走在正确的道路上，这鼓励他们开展更精确、更深奥、更耗费精力的研究。9摆脱了对所有电现象的关注，统一的电学群体可以更加深入地研究特定的现象，为此设计了许多专用设备，并以前所未有的毅力和系统性加以运用。事实收集和理论阐述都变成了高度定向的活动。电学研究的有效性和效率也随之提高，这为弗朗西斯·培根那句精辟的方法论格言提供了社会层面的佐证：“真理更容易从错误中产生，而不是从混乱中产生。” 10

What the fluid theory of electricity did for the subgroup that held it, the Franklinian paradigm later did for the entire group of electricians. It suggested which experiments would be worth performing and which, because directed to secondary or to overly complex manifestations of electricity, would not. Only the paradigm did the job far more effectively, partly because the end of interschool debate ended the constant reiteration of fundamentals and partly because the confidence that they were on the right track encouraged scientists to undertake more precise, esoteric, and consuming sorts of work.9 Freed from the concern with any and all electrical phenomena, the united group of electricians could pursue selected phenomena in far more detail, designing much special equipment for the task and employing it more stubbornly and systematically than electricians had ever done before. Both fact collection and theory articulation became highly directed activities. The effectiveness and efficiency of electrical research increased accordingly, providing evidence for a societal version of Francis Bacon’s acute methodological dictum: “Truth emerges more readily from error than from confusion.”10

我们将在下一节探讨这种高度导向或基于范式的研究的本质，但首先必须简要指出，范式的出现如何影响该领域实践群体的结构。在自然科学的发展过程中，当某个个人或群体首次提出能够吸引大多数下一代实践者的综合理论时，旧学派便会逐渐消失。部分原因是其成员转向了新的范式。但总有一些人坚持某种旧观点，他们最终会被排除在学术界之外，他们的工作也随之被忽视。新的范式意味着对该领域进行新的、更为严格的定义。那些不愿或无法调整自身工作以适应新范式的人，要么只能孤立地开展研究，要么加入其他群体。11历史上，他们往往只是留在哲学系，而许多专门学科正是从哲学系衍生出来的。正如这些迹象所暗示的，有时仅仅是接受某种范式就能将一个原本只对自然研究感兴趣的群体转变为一个职业，或者至少是一个学科。在科学领域（尽管医学、技术和法律等领域并非如此，因为这些领域的主要存在理由是外部社会需求），专业期刊的创办、专家学会的成立以及在课程体系中争取特殊地位，通常都与一个群体首次接受某种范式密切相关。至少在……时期，情况确实如此。一个半世纪前，科学专业化的制度模式首次发展起来；而直到最近，专业化的附属工具才获得了自身的声望。

We shall be examining the nature of this highly directed or paradigm-based research in the next section, but must first note briefly how the emergence of a paradigm affects the structure of the group that practices the field. When, in the development of a natural science, an individual or group first produces a synthesis able to attract most of the next generation’s practitioners, the older schools gradually disappear. In part their disappearance is caused by their members’ conversion to the new paradigm. But there are always some men who cling to one or another of the older views, and they are simply read out of the profession, which thereafter ignores their work. The new paradigm implies a new and more rigid definition of the field. Those unwilling or unable to accommodate their work to it must proceed in isolation or attach themselves to some other group.11 Historically, they have often simply stayed in the departments of philosophy from which so many of the special sciences have been spawned. As these indications hint, it is sometimes just its reception of a paradigm that transforms a group previously interested merely in the study of nature into a profession or, at least, a discipline. In the sciences (though not in fields like medicine, technology, and law, of which the principal raison d’être is an external social need), the formation of specialized journals, the foundation of specialists’ societies, and the claim for a special place in the curriculum have usually been associated with a group’s first reception of a single paradigm. At least this was the case between the time, a century and a half ago, when the institutional pattern of scientific specialization first developed and the very recent time when the paraphernalia of specialization acquired a prestige of their own.

对科学群体的更为僵化的定义会带来其他后果。当科学家可以理所当然地接受某种范式时，他们就不必在主要著作中从零开始构建自己的领域，无需再为引入的每一个概念的运用辩护。这些工作可以留给教科书的作者。然而，有了教科书，富有创造力的科学家就可以从教科书未完成的地方开始研究，从而专注于与其研究领域相关的自然现象中最微妙、最深奥的方面。随着研究的深入，他们的研究成果也会随之改变，这种改变的演变过程鲜为人知，但其现代最终成果却显而易见，甚至令许多人感到压抑。他们的研究成果将不再像富兰克林的《电学实验》或达尔文的《物种起源》那样，以面向所有对该领域感兴趣的人的书籍形式呈现。相反，它们通常会以简短文章的形式出现，仅面向专业同行，这些人被认为具备共同的范式知识，并且只有他们才能阅读写给他们的文章。

The more rigid definition of the scientific group has other consequences. When the individual scientist can take a paradigm for granted, he need no longer, in his major works, attempt to build his field anew, starting from first principles and justifying the use of each concept introduced. That can be left to the writer of textbooks. Given a textbook, however, the creative scientist can begin his research where it leaves off and thus concentrate exclusively upon the subtlest and most esoteric aspects of the natural phenomena that concern his group. And as he does this, his research communiqués will begin to change in ways whose evolution has been too little studied but whose modern end products are obvious to all and oppressive to many. No longer will his researches usually be embodied in books addressed, like Franklin’s Experiments . . . on Electricity or Darwin’s Origin of Species, to anyone who might be interested in the subject matter of the field. Instead they will usually appear as brief articles addressed only to professional colleagues, the men whose knowledge of a shared paradigm can be assumed and who prove to be the only ones able to read the papers addressed to them.

如今在科学领域，书籍通常要么是学术论文，要么是对科学生活某一方面进行回顾性反思的作品。撰写书籍的科学家更有可能发现自己的职业声誉受损而非提升。只有在各科学发展的早期阶段，即范式形成之前的阶段，书籍才像在其他创造性领域那样，与职业成就保持着密切的联系。也只有在那些仍然将书籍（无论是否包含论文）作为研究交流媒介的领域，专业化的界限才仍然如此模糊，以至于外行人可以通过阅读从业者的原始报告来了解研究进展。在数学和天文学领域，研究报告早在古代就已不再为普通受过教育的读者所理解。在动力学领域，研究在中世纪后期也变得类似深奥难懂，但后来又重新获得了大众的理解。这种情况仅在十七世纪初短暂出现过，当时一种新的范式取代了指导中世纪研究的旧范式。到十八世纪末，电学研究开始需要向非专业人士解释，而大多数其他物理科学领域在十九世纪也不再是普通人能够轻易理解的。在同样的两个世纪里，生物科学的各个分支也经历了类似的转变。在社会科学的某些领域，这种转变或许至今仍在发生。尽管人们已经习惯性地（而且当然也理应如此）对专业科学家与其他领域同行之间日益扩大的鸿沟表示惋惜，但对于这种鸿沟与科学进步内在机制之间的本质联系，却关注甚少。

Today in the sciences, books are usually either texts or retrospective reflections upon one aspect or another of the scientific life. The scientist who writes one is more likely to find his professional reputation impaired than enhanced. Only in the earlier, pre-paradigm, stages of the development of the various sciences did the book ordinarily possess the same relation to professional achievement that it still retains in other creative fields. And only in those fields that still retain the book, with or without the article, as a vehicle for research communication are the lines of professionalization still so loosely drawn that the layman may hope to follow progress by reading the practitioners’ original reports. Both in mathematics and astronomy, research reports had ceased already in antiquity to be intelligible to a generally educated audience. In dynamics, research became similarly esoteric in the later Middle Ages, and it recaptured general intelligibility only briefly during the early seventeenth century when a new paradigm replaced the one that had guided medieval research. Electrical research began to require translation for the layman before the end of the eighteenth century, and most other fields of physical science ceased to be generally accessible in the nineteenth. During the same two centuries similar transitions can be isolated in the various parts of the biological sciences. In parts of the social sciences they may well be occurring today. Although it has become customary, and is surely proper, to deplore the widening gulf that separates the professional scientist from his colleagues in other fields, too little attention is paid to the essential relationship between that gulf and the mechanisms intrinsic to scientific advance.

自史前时代以来，各个研究领域不断跨越历史学家所谓的科学史前时期与其真正历史之间的鸿沟。这些走向成熟的转变很少像我那必然带有概括性的论述所暗示的那样突然或明确。但它们也并非是历史性的渐进过程，也就是说，并非与它们所处领域的整体发展同步进行。十八世纪前四十年研究电学的学者掌握的电现象信息远比十六世纪的前辈丰富。1740年后的半个世纪里，他们所列举的新型电现象寥寥无几。然而，在某些重要方面，十八世纪后三分之一时期卡文迪什、库仑和伏特的电学著作与格雷、杜菲甚至富兰克林的著作之间的差异，似乎比这些十八世纪早期电学发现者的著作与十六世纪的著作之间的差异还要大。12大约在1740年至1780年间的某个时候，电工们首次被允许开始学习他们领域的基础知识。理所当然。从那时起，他们开始着手研究更具体、更深奥的问题，并且越来越多地将研究成果发表在面向其他电工的文章中，而不是面向广大学术界的书籍中。作为一个群体，他们取得的成就，堪比古代天文学家、中世纪运动学研究者、17世纪末物理光学研究者以及19世纪初历史地质学研究者。也就是说，他们建立了一种范式，能够指导整个研究团队的研究。除了事后诸葛亮之外，很难找到其他标准能够如此清晰地宣告一个领域是一门科学。

Ever since prehistoric antiquity one field of study after another has crossed the divide between what the historian might call its prehistory as a science and its history proper. These transitions to maturity have seldom been so sudden or so unequivocal as my necessarily schematic discussion may have implied. But neither have they been historically gradual, coextensive, that is to say, with the entire development of the fields within which they occurred. Writers on electricity during the first four decades of the eighteenth century possessed far more information about electrical phenomena than had their sixteenth-century predecessors. During the half-century after 1740, few new sorts of electrical phenomena were added to their lists. Nevertheless, in important respects, the electrical writings of Cavendish, Coulomb, and Volta in the last third of the eighteenth century seem further removed from those of Gray, Du Fay, and even Franklin than are the writings of these early eighteenth-century electrical discoverers from those of the sixteenth century.12 Sometime between 1740 and 1780, electricians were for the first time enabled to take the foundations of their field for granted. From that point they pushed on to more concrete and recondite problems, and increasingly they then reported their results in articles addressed to other electricians rather than in books addressed to the learned world at large. As a group they achieved what had been gained by astronomers in antiquity and by students of motion in the Middle Ages, of physical optics in the late seventeenth century, and of historical geology in the early nineteenth. They had, that is, achieved a paradigm that proved able to guide the whole group’s research. Except with the advantage of hindsight, it is hard to find another criterion that so clearly proclaims a field a science.

[ III ]

[III]

常规科学的本质

The Nature of Normal Science

那么，一个群体接受单一范式后，其所允许的更为专业和深奥的研究的本质是什么？如果该范式代表着一项已经一劳永逸完成的工作，那么它还会给这个联合起来的群体留下哪些需要解决的问题？如果我们注意到迄今为止所使用的术语可能存在误导性，这些问题就显得更加紧迫了。在既定用法中，“范式”指的是一种被接受的模型或模式，正是由于其含义的这一方面，我才得以在此借用“范式”一词（因为我找不到更合适的词）。但很快就会明白，允许我借用“范式”一词的“模型”和“模式”的含义，与通常定义“范式”的含义并不完全相同。例如，在语法中，“ amo, amas, amat ”就是一个范式，因为它展示了许多其他拉丁动词变位所使用的模式，例如，生成“ laudo, laudas, laudat”。在这种标准应用中，范式的作用在于允许复制任何原则上可以替代它的例子。然而，在科学领域，范式很少是复制的对象。相反，它就像普通法中已被接受的司法判决一样，是在新的或更严格的条件下需要进一步阐述和细化的对象。

What then is the nature of the more professional and esoteric research that a group’s reception of a single paradigm permits? If the paradigm represents work that has been done once and for all, what further problems does it leave the united group to resolve? Those questions will seem even more urgent if we now note one respect in which the terms used so far may be misleading. In its established usage, a paradigm is an accepted model or pattern, and that aspect of its meaning has enabled me, lacking a better word, to appropriate ‘paradigm’ here. But it will shortly be clear that the sense of ‘model’ and ‘pattern’ that permits the appropriation is not quite the one usual in defining ‘paradigm.’ In grammar, for example, ‘amo, amas, amat’ is a paradigm because it displays the pattern to be used in conjugating a large number of other Latin verbs, e.g., in producing ‘laudo, laudas, laudat.’ In this standard application, the paradigm functions by permitting the replication of examples any one of which could in principle serve to replace it. In a science, on the other hand, a paradigm is rarely an object for replication. Instead, like an accepted judicial decision in the common law, it is an object for further articulation and specification under new or more stringent conditions.

要了解这是为什么，我们必须认识到这有多么有限。范式在其初次出现时，其范围和精确度都存在差异。范式之所以能获得地位，是因为它们在解决一些被实践者群体公认为十分棘手的问题上，比其他范式更为成功。然而，更成功并非指在单一问题上取得完全成功，或在众多问题上取得显著成功。一个范式的成功——无论是亚里士多德对运动的分析、托勒密对行星位置的计算、拉瓦锡对天平的应用，还是麦克斯韦对电磁场的数学化——在最初阶段，很大程度上是一种成功前景，这种前景只能在一些选定的、尚不完整的例子中发现。常规科学的本质在于实现这种前景，而实现这种前景则需要扩展对那些被范式展现为特别具有启发性的事实的认知，提高这些事实与范式预测之间的匹配程度，并进一步阐明范式本身。

To see how this can be so, we must recognize how very limited in both scope and precision a paradigm can be at the time of its first appearance. Paradigms gain their status because they are more successful than their competitors in solving a few problems that the group of practitioners has come to recognize as acute. To be more successful is not, however, to be either completely successful with a single problem or notably successful with any large number. The success of a paradigm—whether Aristotle’s analysis of motion, Ptolemy’s computations of planetary position, Lavoisier’s application of the balance, or Maxwell’s mathematization of the electromagnetic field—is at the start largely a promise of success discoverable in selected and still incomplete examples. Normal science consists in the actualization of that promise, an actualization achieved by extending the knowledge of those facts that the paradigm displays as particularly revealing, by increasing the extent of the match between those facts and the paradigm’s predictions, and by further articulation of the paradigm itself.

很少有非成熟科学领域的实践者意识到，一个范式会留下多少收尾工作，或者说，这类工作在执行过程中会多么引人入胜。而这些要点需要被理解。收尾工作贯穿了大多数科学家的整个职业生涯。它们构成了我在此所说的常规科学。仔细审视，无论是从历史角度还是在当代实验室中，这种研究似乎都是一种试图将自然强行塞进范式提供的预设且相对僵化的框架中的尝试。常规科学的目标并非在于发现新的现象；事实上，那些无法被框架容纳的现象往往根本不会被发现。科学家通常也不以发明新理论为目标，而且他们往往对他人提出的理论持不宽容的态度。1相反，常规科学研究旨在阐明范式已经提供的那些现象和理论。

Few people who are not actually practitioners of a mature science realize how much mop-up work of this sort a paradigm leaves to be done or quite how fascinating such work can prove in the execution. And these points need to be understood. Mopping-up operations are what engage most scientists throughout their careers. They constitute what I am here calling normal science. Closely examined, whether historically or in the contemporary laboratory, that enterprise seems an attempt to force nature into the preformed and relatively inflexible box that the paradigm supplies. No part of the aim of normal science is to call forth new sorts of phenomena; indeed those that will not fit the box are often not seen at all. Nor do scientists normally aim to invent new theories, and they are often intolerant of those invented by others.1 Instead, normal-scientific research is directed to the articulation of those phenomena and theories that the paradigm already supplies.

或许这些是缺陷。当然，常规科学研究的领域微乎其微；我们现在讨论的这项事业……视野受到极大限制。但这些源于对某种范式的信任的限制，最终却对科学发展至关重要。通过将注意力集中于少数相对深奥的问题上，这种范式迫使科学家们以前所未有的细节和深度去探索自然界的某些方面。而且，常规科学本身就具备一种内在机制，确保一旦其所依赖的范式不再有效运作，限制研究的因素就会随之放松。此时，科学家们的行为方式会发生改变，他们的研究问题也会随之改变。然而，在范式成功的过渡时期，科学界已经解决了许多问题，这些问题是其成员几乎无法想象的，如果没有对该范式的坚持，他们也绝不会着手解决这些问题。而且，至少部分成果总是能够永久保留下来。

Perhaps these are defects. The areas investigated by normal science are, of course, minuscule; the enterprise now under discussion has drastically restricted vision. But those restrictions, born from confidence in a paradigm, turn out to be essential to the development of science. By focusing attention upon a small range of relatively esoteric problems, the paradigm forces scientists to investigate some part of nature in a detail and depth that would otherwise be unimaginable. And normal science possesses a built-in mechanism that ensures the relaxation of the restrictions that bound research whenever the paradigm from which they derive ceases to function effectively. At that point scientists begin to behave differently, and the nature of their research problems changes. In the interim, however, during the period when the paradigm is successful, the profession will have solved problems that its members could scarcely have imagined and would never have undertaken without commitment to the paradigm. And at least part of that achievement always proves to be permanent.

为了更清晰地阐明“常规研究”或“基于范式的研究”的含义，现在让我尝试对常规科学主要包含的问题进行分类和阐述。为方便起见，我暂且搁置理论探讨，先从事实收集入手，也就是科学家们在技术期刊上发表的实验和观察结果，他们通过这些期刊向同行们通报其持续研究的成果。科学家们通常会报告自然界的哪些方面？是什么决定了他们的选择？而且，由于大多数科学观察都需要耗费大量的时间、设备和金钱，是什么激励着科学家们坚持不懈地进行研究并得出结论？

To display more clearly what is meant by normal or paradigm-based research, let me now attempt to classify and illustrate the problems of which normal science principally consists. For convenience I postpone theoretical activity and begin with fact-gathering, that is, with the experiments and observations described in the technical journals through which scientists inform their professional colleagues of the results of their continuing research. On what aspects of nature do scientists ordinarily report? What determines their choice? And, since most scientific observation consumes much time, equipment, and money, what motivates the scientist to pursue that choice to a conclusion?
